research_text:
## Scope and meaning of the finding

`java.security.Signature` provides digital-signature generation and verification for data authentication and integrity. In this finding, the relevant value is the **public-key argument** to `initVerify(PublicKey)`: the reported message says the analysis did not observe the key-generation provenance it expected. That is a detector observation, not a documented Java runtime test that proves the key invalid. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html?utm_source=openai))

## Documented usage and remediation guidance

Oracle documents this sequence: select an explicitly named algorithm with `getInstance`; initialize for signing with a private key or for verification with the signer’s public key or certificate; supply the data with `update`; then call `sign` or `verify`. `verify` returns whether verification succeeded and may throw for improper initialization or an improperly encoded signature. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html?utm_source=openai))  
Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html

For key provenance, Oracle’s examples permit importing an encoded public key with an appropriate `KeyFactory`, or using an existing key and certificate from a keystore. Oracle also advises ensuring that the public key is received intact or using certificates to help authenticate it. The certificate overload extracts its public key and checks a critical X.509 key-usage restriction as documented; the `Signature` API does **not** document that call as performing certificate-path validation. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/security/apisign/vstep2.html?utm_source=openai))  
Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/security/apisign/vstep2.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/security/apisign/enhancements.html

**Remediation limit:** The cited Oracle sources do not prescribe a universal repair for this detector message or require that a verifier locally generate its public key. They document obtaining and authenticating the appropriate signer’s key and using the API correctly. Whether the reported key’s provenance is adequately established, or merely unavailable to the analysis, requires review.

## Compatibility and migration

- **Stored and transmitted signatures:** `Signature` says signature encoding depends on the underlying scheme. Oracle’s standard names distinguish, for example, P1363-format DSA/ECDSA signatures, whose bytes concatenate `r` and `s`, from the documented ASN.1 sequence format for ordinary DSA signatures. A scheme or format change therefore requires compatibility review of stored signatures and communicating peers; the API does not promise that existing bytes remain interchangeable. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/security/Signature.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Keys and parameters:** Oracle’s import example uses an X.509-encoded public key with a matching `KeyFactory`. `RSASSA-PSS` requires explicit PSS parameters before processing data. Algorithm, key, parameter and provider compatibility must be considered separately from the detector’s provenance predicate. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/security/apisign/vstep2.html?utm_source=openai))
- **Platform support:** The Java 8 API lists `SHA256withRSA` among its required algorithms; Java 25 lists additional required algorithms, including specified RSASSA-PSS and ECDSA variants. Support beyond a release’s required set depends on the implementation and providers. Oracle advises general-purpose applications against unnecessarily selecting a specific provider. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/Signature.html))  
  Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/javase/8/docs/api/java/security/Signature.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html
- **Migration path:** The cited `Signature` documentation provides no general automatic migration path for existing signatures or a detector-specific migration. Importing an existing encoded public key is a documented alternative to generating a new key, but compatibility for any particular persisted or wire format is not established by the supplied finding.

## Exact rule in the supplied CrySL source

The relevant matching and requirement clauses are, verbatim:

```crysl
SPEC java.security.Signature
```

```crysl
	java.security.PublicKey publicKey;
	java.security.cert.Certificate cert;
```

```crysl
	i3: initVerify(cert);
	i4: initVerify(publicKey);
```

```crysl
REQUIRES
	generatedPrivkey[privateKey];
	generatedPubkey[publicKey];
```

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/Signature.crysl))

The source specifies `java.security.Signature` as the governed type and two **one-argument** `initVerify` events, with variables declared as `Certificate` and `PublicKey`. The reported provenance requirement is `generatedPubkey[publicKey]`; the certificate variable has no corresponding provenance requirement in the shown `REQUIRES` block.

**A method name alone is not the match stated by this rule:** it specifies `java.security.Signature`, not an arbitrary unrelated receiver with a same-named method. The file does not itself specify detector dispatch or subtype-matching details, so those cannot be resolved from this source alone.

The supplied URL points to a mutable branch. The retrieved text contains the clauses above, but this research pass did **not** independently verify its bytes against the supplied SHA-256.
